Between December 2024 and November 2026, Canada enacted the most expansive structural overhaul of its flagship Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentive program in more than a decade. Initiated in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 16, 2024), expanded in Budget 2025 (November 4, 2025), enacted into law via Bill C-15 (S.C. 2026, c. 3, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026), and proposed to be further broadened in Budget 2026 (November 2026), these reforms fundamentally altered corporate eligibility, expenditure caps, capital asset treatment, commercialisation support, and upfront administrative certainty. Concurrently, at the provincial level, Québec abolished eight legacy R&D and innovation tax credit programs for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, replacing them with the unified, fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC).
1. Executive Summary and Legislative Landscape (2024–2026 Reforms)

Canada's federal SR&ED program operates under a dual-incentive statutory mechanism established in the federal Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.). First, Section 37 of the ITA permits taxpayers carrying on business in Canada to pool and immediately deduct 100% of allowable current—and, for property acquired after December 15, 2024, allowable capital—SR&ED expenditures against business income, or carry those unclaimed deductions forward indefinitely. Second, Sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA provide an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) ranging from a 15% basic rate to an enhanced 35% rate on qualified SR&ED expenditures, which can reduce Part I federal income tax payable, generate a direct cash refund, or be carried back 3 taxation years and forward 20 taxation years.
Chronology and Scope of the 2024–2026 Federal SR&ED Reforms
Tax practitioners, corporate controllers, and R&D auditors must distinguish carefully between the initial policy announcements in late 2024 and the final statutory provisions enacted in 2026:

items: The 2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 16, 2024): The Department of Finance initially proposed a $1.9 billion six-year investment to modernize the SR&ED program effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (that is, after December 15, 2024). That initial proposal sought to raise the expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3.0 million to $4.5 million, expand the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extend the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) using a three-year average gross revenue phase-out, allow Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) to elect into the gross revenue phase-out regime, and restore the eligibility of SR&ED capital expenditures and equipment lease costs.

Budget 2025 (November 4, 2025) and Bill C-15 (Royal Assent March 26, 2026): Tabled on November 4, 2025, by the Minister of Finance and National Revenue, François-Philippe Champagne, Budget 2025 superseded the $4.5 million interim proposal and doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% SR&ED ITC from $3.0 million to $6.0 million, retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. This expansion increased the maximum annual enhanced refundable cash credit on current expenditures from $1,050,000 ($3.0 million × 35%) to $2,100,000 ($6.0 million × 35%). Budget 2025 projected an incremental fiscal cost of $293 million over five years ($3 million in 2025–2026, $70 million in 2026–2027, $85 million in 2027–2028, $65 million in 2028–2029, and $70 million in 2029–2030) for the jump from $4.5 million to $6.0 million. The implementing legislation, Bill C-15 (An Act to implement certain provisions of the budget tabled in Parliament on November 4, 2025), received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, as S.C. 2026, c. 3.

2026 Spring Economic Update and Administrative Modernization (April 2026): To address long-standing industry concerns regarding post-filing audit uncertainty, the federal government and the CRA launched a streamlined four-step SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval process in April 2026, providing formal upfront eligibility determinations within eight weeks of application submission in My Business Account. Federal economic modelling projects that the combined SR&ED enhancements will generate $1.2 billion annually in incremental economic output.

Budget 2026 Commercialisation Expansion and Innovation Package (November 2026): In Budget 2026, the federal government proposed a $930 million five-year expansion ($25 million in 2026–2027, $200 million in 2027–2028, $245 million in 2028–2029, $225 million in 2029–2030, and $235 million in 2030–2031, with $235 million ongoing) to broaden the SR&ED program into commercialisation expenses for taxation years beginning on or after Budget Day. Under this proposed measure, eligible activities and expenditures would be expanded to cover costs associated with bringing a new product or process to market, specifically obtaining necessary regulatory approvals or certifications and securing and maintaining intellectual property (IP) protection. Budget 2026 also confirmed the proposed Productivity Mega Deduction—allowing immediate 100% capital expensing across more than 65% of business investments and reducing Canada's marginal effective tax rate (METR) on new business investment from 13.0% to 6.4%, the lowest in the G7—alongside Patent Act transparency and demand-letter reforms and $1 billion in renewed funding for the Strategic Response Fund (SRF) (formerly the Strategic Innovation Fund).

body.text: 2. Statutory Architecture and Scientific Eligibility Framework
The Statutory Definition of SR&ED: Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

The legal gatekeeper for all federal—and harmonized provincial—R&D tax incentives in Canada is the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED means a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis, and encompasses four distinct statutory limbs across paragraphs (a) through (d).

First, basic research under paragraph 248(1)(a) comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. Basic research typically takes place in laboratory or academic settings and often results in peer-reviewed scientific publications, such as characterizing the properties of elementary particles (for example, the discovery of the electron) or studying a newly discovered virus to understand its fundamental biological characteristics.

Second, applied research under paragraph 248(1)(b) comprises work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Applied research seeks to generate new scientific knowledge directed toward an industrial, medical, or commercial objective prior to building a specific commercial device or process—for example, investigating how electrons behave in semiconductor materials to establish the physical principle of a transistor, or exploiting characteristics of a newly discovered virus to develop a candidate vaccine.

Third, experimental development under paragraph 248(1)(c) comprises work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. The vast majority of industrial, manufacturing, and software SR&ED claims in Canada fall under paragraph (c). Crucially, the statute explicitly covers incremental improvements to existing products or processes (such as scaling up and optimizing processes to enable rapid, large-scale vaccine production), provided the work seeks a genuine technological advancement rather than routine commercial engineering.

Fourth, eligible support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) comprises work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to eight exhaustive statutory categories—namely engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—where that work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Support work does not constitute SR&ED on its own; its eligibility is strictly derivative and requires demonstrating that the amount, size, extent, and duration of the activity corresponded directly to the needs of resolving the core scientific or technological uncertainty.
Statutorily Excluded Work: Paragraphs 248(1)(e) to (k)

Subsection 248(1) explicitly carves out seven categories of commercial, routine, and non-scientific activities in paragraphs (e) through (k), collectively termed "excluded work" by the CRA. Even if conducted within an innovative enterprise, work with respect to any of the following cannot be claimed as SR&ED:

items: Paragraph (e): Market research or sales promotion;
Paragraph (f): Quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes;
Paragraph (g): Research in the social sciences or the humanities;

Paragraph (h): Prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas (note that while upstream prospecting or drilling is excluded, experimental development of new extraction or processing technologies remains eligible if separated from prospecting);
Paragraph (i): The commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product, or the commercial use of a new or improved process;
Paragraph (j): Style changes (modifications that are purely aesthetic or cosmetic without underlying technological advancement); and

Paragraph (k): Routine data collection (unless the data collection is carried out specifically to directly support and is commensurate with the needs of basic research, applied research, or experimental development under paragraph (d)).

body.text: Furthermore, CRA administrative guidance confirms that activities aimed merely at acquiring knowledge or know-how that already exists in the public domain or industry—such as general employee training, on-the-job learning, hiring experts (employees or consultants) simply to apply what they already know, or purchasing proprietary knowledge—do not attempt to achieve a scientific or technological advancement and are therefore ineligible. In software and artificial intelligence development, industry and CRA guidance similarly distinguishes between eligible experimental development under technological uncertainty and ineligible routine software engineering such as writing integrations with external APIs using vendor-provided documentation, routine debugging, user interface design, or prompt engineering against existing foundation models.
Evolution of CRA Eligibility Guidance: From the "Five Questions" to the "Why and How" Requirements

In evaluating whether a project satisfies subsection 248(1), tax auditors must understand the relationship between the CRA's current administrative guidelines and the underlying common-law test established by the courts. Under the CRA's former Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (dated April 24, 2015, now archived), the CRA evaluated projects using a two-step methodology centred on "Five Questions" derived from the landmark Tax Court of Canada decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839:

items: Was there a scientific or a technological uncertainty?
Did the effort involve formulating hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that uncertainty?
Was the overall approach adopted consistent with a systematic investigation or search, including formulating and testing the hypotheses by means of experiment or analysis?
Was the overall approach undertaken for the purpose of achieving a scientific or a technological advancement?
Was a record of the hypotheses tested and the results kept as the work progressed?

body.text: On August 13, 2021, the CRA replaced the 2015 policy document with the Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives. The 2021 Guidelines reorganize the five questions into two overarching statutory requirements—the "Why" Requirement and the "How" Requirement—both of which must be satisfied simultaneously.

Under the "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Advancement and Uncertainty), work must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. A scientific or technological advancement requires attempting to generate or discover new knowledge that advances the understanding of science or technology because the claimant encountered a scientific or technological uncertainty—meaning a problem, limitation, or capability gap where existing scientific knowledge, standard practice, or routine engineering could not predict whether a given objective could be achieved or how to achieve it. Crucially, system uncertainty qualifies even where individual components or publicly available solutions are known, provided their integration or application in a novel context creates unpredictable technological constraints that cannot be resolved through standard procedures. Equally important, a project does not need to succeed commercially or technically to satisfy the "Why" requirement; discovering through systematic testing why a hypothesized approach fails generates new technological knowledge and reinforces the existence of the technological uncertainty.

Under the "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search), work must be conducted by means of a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis, performed by qualified individuals (personnel with relevant qualifications and/or experience in science, technology, or engineering). The CRA's 2021 Guidelines specify that satisfying the "How" requirement demands four concrete operational steps: (1) defining a problem and generating a hypothesis (an idea consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward resolving the scientific or technological uncertainty); (2) testing the hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis, allowing the hypothesis to evolve and change as a result of testing; (3) developing logical conclusions based on the results or findings of the experiment or analysis; and (4) keeping contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses (such as lab notebooks, test logs, commit histories, issue tickets, mathematical models, and failure analyses) that links the hypotheses tested to the results obtained.

As confirmed by the CRA's A brief history of the guidance on the eligibility of work (updated August 27, 2025) and by the Federal Court of Appeal in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88, and National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72, the transition from the "Five Questions" to the "Why and How" framework is purely an administrative simplification of language; the statutory definition in subsection 248(1) did not change, and the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria remain the authoritative legal standard enforced by Canadian courts.
Project Definition, Production Runs, and Custom Assets

Under CRA policy and Guide T4088, an "SR&ED project" is defined at the level of a set of interrelated activities that collectively are necessary to resolve specific scientific or technological uncertainties in an attempt to achieve defined scientific or technological advancements. Where experimental development occurs in an industrial or manufacturing environment, two specialized CRA policies govern the boundary between eligible SR&ED under paragraph 248(1)(c)/(d) and excluded commercial production under paragraph 248(1)(i).

First, under the SR&ED During Production Runs Policy (covering Experimental Production vs. Commercial Production), when a business conducts experimental development simultaneously with a production run (ED+EP or ED+CP), all costs normally incurred for standard commercial production—and any excess production beyond what is strictly necessary to validate the experimental hypothesis—must be excluded from the claim. Only the incremental or excess costs directly associated with the experimental development work (and materials consumed or transformed in the experimental phase) are allowable. In multi-stage continuous manufacturing processes, only the specific process steps undergoing experimental development (and necessary upstream input material costs transformed during that experimental step) qualify, subject to ITC recapture if the resulting output is sold or converted to commercial use.

Second, under the SR&ED while Developing an Asset Policy (covering Pilot Plants, Prototypes, and Custom Commercial Assets), where a claimant constructs a pilot plant (a non-commercial scale facility operated to resolve technological uncertainties and acquire technological knowledge), the labour and materials consumed or transformed in building and operating the pilot plant qualify as SR&ED. Conversely, where a claimant develops a custom commercial product or internal commercial plant/asset that incorporates experimental development, the allowable SR&ED expenditure is limited to: (a) the total actual costs of developing the custom product or commercial asset minus the estimated costs that would normally be associated with constructing the asset had the technology already existed, plus (b) an estimated amount representing the cost of materials transformed in the specific components where SR&ED occurred (which then become subject to ITC recapture upon commercial use or sale).
3. Federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, and Refundability Mechanics

The calculation, allocation, phase-out, and refundability of federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credits are governed by Section 127 (specifically subsections 127(5), 127(8), 127(9), and 127(10.1) to 127(10.64)) and Section 127.1 (specifically subsections 127.1(1), 127.1(2), 127.1(2.01), and 127.1(3)) of the Income Tax Act.
Basic Rate (15%) vs. Enhanced Rate (35%)

Under the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9), the baseline federal SR&ED ITC rate is 15% of a taxpayer's "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool" at the end of the taxation year. This 15% basic rate applies to: (a) all corporations that do not qualify for the enhanced rate, such as foreign-controlled corporations, non-qualifying public corporations, and large corporations whose expenditure limit has been phased out; (b) qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs on the portion of their annual qualified SR&ED expenditures that exceeds their annual expenditure limit for the taxation year; and (c) unincorporated businesses (sole proprietorships / individuals), partners of partnerships (allocated under subsection 127(8)), and beneficiaries of trusts.

Under subsection 127(10.1), an additional 20% ITC is added to the 15% basic rate—yielding a combined enhanced ITC rate of 35%—on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the corporation's annual expenditure limit. For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the 35% enhanced rate was restricted exclusively to Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) (as defined in subsection 125(7) of the ITA) up to a maximum annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024), pursuant to Bill C-15 (S.C. 2026, c. 3), the 35% enhanced rate applies to both CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) up to a maximum annual expenditure limit of $6,000,000.
Statutory Definition of an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC)

To qualify as an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) under the new definition in subsection 127(9) of the ITA (effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024), a corporation must satisfy four cumulative statutory conditions throughout the taxation year:

items: Canadian Residency (Subparagraph (a)(i)): The corporation is resident in Canada;

Public Status (Subparagraph (a)(ii)): The corporation is a "public corporation" (as defined in subsection 89(1) of the ITA) or is a corporation a class of the capital stock of which is listed on a designated stock exchange;

Absence of Direct or Indirect Non-Resident Control (Subparagraph (a)(iii)): The corporation is not controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever (within the meaning of subsection 256(5.1) de facto and de jure control), by one or more non-resident persons; and

Hypothetical Non-Resident Shareholder Test (Subparagraph (a)(iv)): The corporation would not, if each share of its capital stock (or of the capital stock of another corporation) that is owned by a non-resident person were owned by a single particular hypothetical person, be controlled by that particular person (parallel to paragraph (b) of the CCPC definition in subsection 125(7), ensuring that dispersed non-resident shareholdings do not exceed 50% of voting power in the aggregate).

body.text: Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas: Taxable Capital vs. Gross Revenue

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 maximum annual expenditure limit is subject to two distinct statutory phase-out mechanisms under subsections 127(10.2) and 127(10.6) of the ITA.
1. The Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula (CCPC Default: Subsection 127(10.2))

Unless a CCPC elects to use the gross revenue method, its annual expenditure limit is determined by the taxable capital employed in Canada (within the meaning of Part I.3 / section 181.2 of the ITA) of the CCPC and all associated corporations for the immediately preceding taxation year. Where prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $15,000,000 or less (increased from $10,000,000 for pre-December 16, 2024 taxation years), the CCPC retains the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit. Where prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 (increased from $10,000,000–$50,000,000), the $6,000,000 limit is reduced on a straight-line basis by $1.00 for every $10.00 of taxable capital in excess of $15,000,000:
Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 − [(prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada − $15,000,000) ÷ 10]

Where prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada reaches $75,000,000 or more (increased from $50,000,000), the expenditure limit is reduced to nil ($0), and all qualified expenditures earn the 15% basic rate. Furthermore, for purposes of determining whether a CCPC is a "qualifying corporation" under subsection 127.1(2) (which governs 40% refundability on the 15% basic credit above the expenditure limit), the corporation's prior-year taxable income must not exceed its "qualifying income limit", which is updated for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, to the formula:

where A is nil if prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is $15,000,000 or less, and in any other case is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which prior-year taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000 (phasing out to nil at $75,000,000).
2. The 3-Year Average Gross Revenue Phase-Out Formula (ECPC Mandatory & CCPC Elective: Subsections 127(10.6), 127(10.32), and 127(10.64))

Because public corporations and venture-backed technology or life-sciences companies frequently raise substantial equity or debt capital (inflating their balance-sheet taxable capital above $15 million before generating significant commercial revenue), Bill C-15 enacted subsection 127(10.6) to base the expenditure limit phase-out on average annual gross revenue. This gross revenue test is mandatory for ECPCs and elective for CCPCs (and associated CCPC groups filing an election under subsection 127(10.32) using the prescribed form, which disapplies the subsection 127(10.2) taxable capital test for that taxation year).

Average annual revenue is computed as the average of the annual gross revenue reflected in the financial statements of the corporation—or, for a consolidated ECPC group, reflected in the consolidated financial statements of the group, or summed across all associated CCPCs regardless of whether they were associated throughout the entire period—over the 3 preceding fiscal years (or over the actual 1 or 2 preceding fiscal years if the corporation has fewer than 3 preceding fiscal years, pursuant to subsection 127(10.64)). While August 2025 draft legislative notes initially referenced the $4.5 million FES cap, Budget 2025 and enacted Bill C-15 set the maximum expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.6) at $6,000,000, phasing out linearly when 3-year average annual gross revenue is between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, and becoming nil ($0) at $75,000,000 or more.
3. Associated CCPCs, Consolidated ECPCs, and Short Taxation Years

Under subsections 127(10.21), 127(10.3), and 127(10.4), associated CCPCs must share a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit and file Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit). If the associated group fails to file the allocation agreement within 30 days after a written request by the Minister of National Revenue, the Minister allocates the limit among the group under subsection 127(10.4). Parallel rules in subsections 127(10.61), 127(10.62), and 127(10.63) require ECPCs that are members of a consolidated group preparing consolidated financial statements to share a single $6,000,000 expenditure limit, allocate it by filing an election with the Minister under subsection 127(10.62), and submit to Ministerial allocation under subsection 127(10.63) if not filed within 30 days of request.

Where a corporation has a taxation year of less than 51 weeks, or where a corporation has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year while associated with another corporation, its allocated expenditure limit is prorated by the ratio of the number of days in the short taxation year to 365 under subsection 127(10.5) (formerly numbered 127(10.6)). For example, a CCPC allocated $3,000,000 of a group's limit that has a second short taxation year running 184 days from July 1 to December 31 has its expenditure limit for that short taxation year prorated to $3,000,000 × (184 ÷ 365) = $1,512,329.
Comprehensive Refundability Matrix (Section 127.1 ITA)

Under Section 127.1 of the ITA, any portion of a taxpayer's SR&ED ITC that is not used to offset Part I federal income tax payable in the current year (or carried back up to 3 years) may qualify as a "refundable investment tax credit" under subsections 127.1(2) and 127.1(2.01). Any ITC refunded to the taxpayer is deemed under subsection 127.1(3) to have been deducted against Part I tax, thereby reducing the unused ITC pool available for carryforward (up to 20 years) and reducing the following year's Section 37 deductible expenditure pool. A critical technical nuance of the post-December 15, 2024 rules is that capital expenditures earn a 40% refund rate rather than a 100% refund rate, even when the ITC is earned at the 35% enhanced rate:

body.text: Illustrative Calculation: CCPC vs. ECPC with $8,000,000 in Qualified Current Expenditures (2025/2026)

To see how these rules operate in practice, consider a Qualifying CCPC and an ECPC, each with $10 million in prior-year taxable capital and $10 million in 3-year average gross revenue (entitling both to the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit), and each incurring $8,000,000 in qualified current SR&ED expenditures with zero Part I tax payable. On the first $6,000,000 of qualified current expenditures within the expenditure limit, both the Qualifying CCPC and the ECPC earn the 35% enhanced rate ($6,000,000 × 35% = $2,100,000), which is 100% refundable in cash ($2,100,000). On the remaining $2,000,000 of qualified current expenditures above the expenditure limit, both corporations earn the 15% basic rate ($2,000,000 × 15% = $300,000). For the Qualifying CCPC, 40% of that basic ITC is refundable in cash ($300,000 × 40% = $120,000 cash refund, with the remaining $180,000 carried back 3 years or forward 20 years as a non-refundable credit), yielding a total cash refund of $2,220,000. For the ECPC, 0% of the basic ITC above $6,000,000 is refundable (the entire $300,000 above the limit is non-refundable), yielding a total cash refund of $2,100,000 plus $300,000 in non-refundable ITC carryforwards.
4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Methodological Elections: Traditional vs. Proxy Method
The Irrevocable Annual Election: Traditional vs. Proxy Method (Subsection 37(10) ITA)

When filing Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim), a claimant must elect on Line 160 (Proxy Method) or Line 162 (Traditional Method) how to compute its SR&ED expenditures for the taxation year. Under subsection 37(10) of the ITA and the CRA's Traditional and Proxy Methods Policy, this election is made annually on the first Form T661 filed for the taxation year and is strictly irrevocable for that taxation year once submitted. If a claimant fails to select a method on Form T661, the CRA automatically processes the claim using the Traditional Method.

body.text: Salaries and Wages: Directly Engaged Personnel vs. Specified Employees

Under the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy, "salary or wages" is defined in subsection 248(1) of the ITA as income from an office or employment computed under Subdivision a of Division B of Part I (Sections 5 to 8 of the ITA), including vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, director's or management fees, commissions, and taxable benefits (where there is a cash outlay or reasonable estimate of actual employer cost excluding GST/HST/PST input tax credits), but explicitly excluding superannuation or pension benefits, retiring allowances, extended vacation or sick leave, employer-paid payroll benefit contributions, and employee stock option benefits (excluded under section 7 and subsections 143.3(2)–(5) of the ITA).
1. Directly Engaged Tasks vs. Non-Eligible Tasks

Whether an employee is "directly engaged" in SR&ED is a question of fact based on the duties performed, not the job title of the employee. Eligible directly engaged tasks include hands-on scientific research or experimental development experiments, coding, prototyping, and mathematical analysis performed by qualified individuals; first-line technical supervision and technological planning for ongoing claimed SR&ED projects (such as assigning technological personnel, setting job priorities, developing technological strategies, or evaluating the quality of materials used); and hands-on tasks performed by non-specialized employees when supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications, such as operating a machine required for an experiment or feeding raw materials into an experimental run. Long-term corporate strategic planning, contract administration, and clerical/administrative support are not considered "directly engaged" in SR&ED (they are covered by the PPA under the Proxy Method, or claimed as overhead on Line 360 under the Traditional Method if directly related and incremental). Furthermore, salaries or drawings paid to sole proprietors or partners of a partnership are not employment salaries or wages and cannot be claimed.
2. Specified Employees: Definition and Three-Tier Statutory Limitations

A "specified employee" is defined in subsection 248(1) of the ITA as an employee of a taxpayer who is either: (a) a "specified shareholder" of the taxpayer—meaning a person who owns, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the corporation or of any corporation related to the corporation—or (b) a person who does not deal at arm's length with the taxpayer under section 251 of the ITA. Because owner-managers and non-arm's length family members can influence their own compensation structures, the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations impose three strict statutory limitations on specified employees:

items: Absolute Prohibition on Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration (Subsection 37(9) ITA): Unlike arm's-length (non-specified) employees—whose bonuses and remuneration based on profits (reported on Line 812 of Form T661) are fully allowable in the Section 37 deductible pool and earn direct ITCs—a specified employee cannot claim any bonus or remuneration based on profits as an SR&ED expenditure under either the Traditional or Proxy Method.

Maximum Deductible SR&ED Salary Cap: 5 × YMPE (Subsections 37(9.1) to 37(9.5) ITA): Under subsection 37(9.1), the maximum amount of a specified employee's salary or wages that can be included in the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool (and earn direct salary ITCs) is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the individual was a specified employee. If the specified employee is employed by two or more associated corporations, no amount may be claimed unless the corporations file Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)), accompanied by a certified copy of the directors' resolution authorizing the agreement (or a signed confirmation if owned by a single sole shareholder), allocating the 5 × YMPE limit among them.

PPA Salary Base Cap for Specified Employees: Lesser of 75% of Total Salary or 2.5 × YMPE (Subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) ITR): When calculating the salary base for the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount in Part 5 of Form T661 (Box 856), the maximum amount included for each specified employee is restricted to the lesser of: (a) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages for the year (SR&ED and non-SR&ED combined, excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year); and (b) 2.5 × YMPE × (Days employed in year ÷ 365) (note that under subsection 2900(7), this proration is based on total days employed in the taxation year, without proration for days the employee was not a specified employee, and must be shared across associated corporations under subsection 2900(8)).
