body.text: 3. Foreign SR&ED Salaries (Subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) ITA)

While SR&ED expenditures must generally be carried on in Canada (including Canada's exclusive economic zone, airspace, seabed, and subsoil under the Oceans Act pursuant to subsection 37(1.3)), subsections 37(1.4) and 37(1.5) permit a taxpayer to claim permissible salary or wages paid to employees performing SR&ED work outside Canada where four cumulative conditions are met: (i) the work was carried on outside Canada; (ii) the work was directly undertaken by the taxpayer (foreign subcontractors do not qualify); (iii) the work related to a business of the taxpayer; and (iv) the work was solely in support of SR&ED carried on in Canada by the taxpayer. The maximum permissible foreign SR&ED salary (reported on Line 307 for non-specified employees and Line 309 for specified employees of Form T661) is strictly capped at 10% of the total SR&ED salary or wages incurred for SR&ED carried on in Canada (Line 306 of Form T661).
The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) and the Overall PPA Cap (Subsections 2900(4)–(10) ITR)

Under the Proxy Method, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is calculated on Line 820 of Part 5, Section B of Form T661 as 55% of the eligible salary base. For all employees (both specified and non-specified), subsection 2900(9) of the Income Tax Regulations requires excluding from the PPA salary base: (1) taxable benefits under section 6 of the ITA, (2) stock option benefits under section 7 of the ITA, (3) bonuses, (4) remuneration based on profits, (5) employer-paid payroll benefit contributions, and (6) unpaid remuneration from a prior taxation year paid in the current taxation year (Line 310 of Form T661, including reasonable vacation/holiday pay or salary deferral arrangements excluded from the salary base).

Furthermore, under subsection 2900(6) of the Income Tax Regulations, the PPA cannot exceed the Overall Cap on the PPA, which ensures that the notional PPA does not exceed the taxpayer's actual non-SR&ED business deductions for the year. The Overall PPA Cap is calculated by the formula:
Overall PPA Cap = A − B − C

In this formula, A is the total of all amounts deducted in computing the taxpayer's net income for tax purposes from the business for the year (including cost of goods sold, and summed across all businesses if the taxpayer carries on more than one business); B is the total of all specific statutory deductions claimed in the year under Section 20 (such as Capital Cost Allowance, interest expense, and bad debts), Section 24 (ceasing to carry on business), Section 26 (banks), Section 30 (improving land for farming), Section 32 (insurance agents and brokers), Section 37 (the SR&ED deduction claimed on Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1), Sections 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development resource expenses), and Section 104 (trusts); and C is the total amount of expenditures incurred in the year for the use of, or the right to use, a building (building rent or lease expenses).
Overhead and Other Expenditures Under the Traditional Method (Subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) ITR)

Claimants electing the Traditional Method do not compute a PPA; instead, they claim actual overhead and other expenditures on Line 360 of Form T661. Under subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(II) of the ITA and subsections 2900(2) and 2900(3) of the Income Tax Regulations, an overhead expenditure qualifies only if it is "directly attributable" to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (or to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada), which requires proving on audit that the expense meets both the Directly Related Test (a direct linkage without an intervening step or intermediary to the SR&ED work, SR&ED staff, or SR&ED machinery/equipment) and the Incremental Test (the expenditure, or the claimed incremental portion thereof, would not have been incurred had the SR&ED prosecution not occurred). Fixed costs that do not vary with SR&ED usage (such as fixed-cost annual maintenance contracts) and waste disposal costs incurred after the SR&ED activity has finished fail the incremental test. Similarly, while moving and relocation expenses to transfer SR&ED candidates or hands-on SR&ED employees within Canada (and related taxable housing-loss benefits) qualify under the Traditional Method if directly related and incremental, pre-employment recruitment costs—specifically headhunter fees, job advertising, interview travel, and work permit/immigration fees—are excluded as ordinary business expenses.

Auditors must also enforce Section 2902 of the Income Tax Regulations, which designates specific items as "prescribed expenditures" that cannot earn an SR&ED ITC even if they appear related to R&D. Specifically, subparagraph 2902(a)(i) excludes general administration or management expenses; clause 2902(a)(i)(B) excludes legal or accounting fees—including all fees paid to external accountants or third-party SR&ED consultants for preparing Form T661 (whereas internal salary or wages paid to the claimant's own employees for preparing the SR&ED claim remain allowable under the exception in Clause 2902(a)(i)(A) if directly related and incremental); clause 2902(a)(i)(C) excludes interest and financing costs; and clause 2902(a)(i)(F) excludes costs to attend technical conventions and conferences. Paragraphs 2902(c), (d), and (e) also prescribe expenditures to acquire rights in or arising out of SR&ED, charitable donations under sections 110.1 or 118.1, and reimbursed expenditures.
Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed (Materials for SR&ED Policy)

Under both the Traditional Method (Paragraph 2900(2)(a) ITR) and the Proxy Method (Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V) ITA), a claimant may include 100% of the laid-down cost (invoice cost, customs and excise duties, transportation, acquisition and storage costs, and, for self-manufactured inventory, direct labour and GAAP production overhead) of materials consumed or materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. Under the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, "materials for SR&ED" means raw materials, substances, or other items that are physical and tangible (solid, liquid, or gaseous) and that compose the body of a tangible thing at a given moment in the SR&ED process (either the tangible object on which SR&ED is carried out or the tangible object resulting from the SR&ED). Consequently, laboratory supplies and glassware (beakers, test tubes, pipettes, petri dishes), cleaning supplies, general utilities (electricity, water, natural gas), CDs/DVDs, software licences, and intangible data do not qualify as materials consumed or transformed (unless they are the physical subject of the SR&ED itself).

While some third-party startup guides and practitioner blogs loosely group R&D cloud computing expenses (such as AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud compute instances used to train AI models or run experimental staging environments) under materials, under strict CRA statutory interpretation intangible cloud services do not satisfy the physical-matter requirement of the Materials for SR&ED Policy. Instead, under the CRA's SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 2026) and SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, dedicated R&D computer hardware leases and telecommunications bandwidth qualify as equipment lease costs (for amounts payable after December 15, 2024) or as directly related and incremental telecommunications/internet overhead under the Traditional Method (or are absorbed under the 55% PPA under the Proxy Method). In all cases, claimants must maintain separate cost accounts to segregate R&D/development cloud infrastructure from commercial production infrastructure.

The CRA distinguishes sharply between materials consumed (reported on Line 320 of Form T661), which are materials destroyed or rendered virtually valueless (resale or scrap value ≤ 10% of original cost) as a result of the SR&ED, and materials transformed (reported on Line 325 of Form T661), which are materials changed or incorporated into another physical object (such as a prototype, experimental production batch, or custom asset) that retains value exceeding 10% of its original cost. Materials can only be claimed in the taxation year in which they are actually consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED (not when purchased into inventory), and materials transformed are subject to ITC recapture if sold or converted to commercial use within 20 years.
Subcontractors (Arm's-Length vs. Non-Arm's-Length) and Third-Party Payments

Where a claimant contracts an arm's-length taxable supplier (a person resident in Canada or a non-resident carrying on business through a permanent establishment in Canada) to perform SR&ED on its behalf in Canada under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) and subparagraph (a)(ii) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9), 100% of the eligible contract expenditure is added to the Section 37 deductible pool (Line 340 of Form T661), and 80% qualifies for the SR&ED ITC (a 20% statutory reduction is deducted on Line 529 of Form T661). If an arm's-length contract includes both SR&ED and non-SR&ED work for a single price, the claimant must make a reasonable allocation based on fair market value. An arm's-length payer may also claim contract expenditures for eligible support work under paragraph 248(1)(d) if that support work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of SR&ED performed by or on behalf of the payer in Canada (though the arm's-length contractor cannot claim SR&ED on support work alone). If an SR&ED contract is paid to a non-taxable supplier (such as a foreign contractor without a Canadian permanent establishment), 0% qualifies for the ITC (deducted on Line 528 of Form T661).

Where a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's-length (NAL) performer (Line 345 of Form T661), paragraph (f) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) allows the payment in the payer's Section 37 deductible pool, but excludes 100% of the NAL contract payment from the payer's qualified expenditures for ITC purposes. Under subsection 37(13), work performed by a taxpayer for a non-arm's-length person or partnership is deemed to be SR&ED if it would be SR&ED had it been performed by that person or partnership (enabling an NAL performer to claim support work performed for an NAL payer). The NAL performer can either claim the ITCs directly on its own underlying expenditures (and the amount received from the NAL payer is not a "contract payment" that reduces the performer's claim), or the NAL performer (transferor) and NAL payer (transferee) can jointly file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsection 127(13) to transfer the performer's qualified expenditures (capped at the contract amount) to the payer (reported on Line 540 by the performer and Line 546 by the payer). Note that a partnership cannot transfer or receive qualified expenditures under Form T1146. Additionally, where a claimant purchases goods, materials, or capital property from a non-arm's-length supplier, subsection 127(11.6) limits the qualified expenditure for ITC purposes to the adjusted selling cost or adjusted service cost to the NAL supplier, eliminating any inter-company profit (adjusted on Line 543 of Form T661).

Under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1), (ii), and (iii) and the CRA's Third-Party Payments Policy, payments made to eligible Canadian third-party research entities—categorized by the CRA as "A to F entities" (A: Canadian-resident corporations; B: approved associations; C: approved universities, colleges, or research institutes; D: paragraph 149(1)(j) non-profit SR&ED corporations; E: approved granting councils CIHR, NSERC, and SSHRC; and F: paragraph 149(1)(j) non-profit R&D consortia conducting basic or applied research relevant to the corporate payer's SR&ED)—where the claimant is entitled to exploit the results in Canada are reported on Line 370 of Form T661 and detailed on Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)). Unlike contract SR&ED (where the payer controls the work and owns exclusive rights), third-party payments involve research controlled by the performing institution where the payer receives non-exclusive or preferential rights to exploit the results. Like arm's-length contracts, 100% of a third-party payment enters the Section 37 deductible pool, and 80% qualifies for the SR&ED ITC (subject to the 20% reduction on Line 529 of Form T661).
5. Restoration of Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE), and Lease Costs

From January 1, 2014, through December 15, 2024, all capital expenditures and equipment lease payments were excluded from the SR&ED program. Effective for depreciable property acquired (and available for use) after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024) and lease costs that first become payable after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 (S.C. 2026, c. 3, s. 5) restored paragraph 37(1)(b), amended subsections 37(6), 37(6.1), 37(8), and 127(9), and repealed the capital look-through rules in former subsections 37(14) and 37(15) (which previously required reducing contract and third-party payments by any capital expenditures incurred by the performer).
1. All or Substantially All (ASA, ≥ 90%) Capital Expenditures (Paragraph 37(1)(b) ITA)

Under the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (revised June 29, 2026), an expenditure to acquire depreciable property after December 15, 2024, qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure on Line 390 of Form T661 (under Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(III) for the Traditional Method and Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(III) for the Proxy Method) if, at the time it was incurred and became available for use (Subsection 37(1.2) and Subsection 13(27) ITA), the claimant intended that the property would either: (1) be used during All or Substantially All (ASA, meaning 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life for the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada (Operating Time Test); or (2) have ASA (90% or more) of its value consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada (Value Test).

Under subsection 37(6), any capital expenditure deducted under subsection 37(1) is deemed to be Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) allowed to the taxpayer. Consequently, capital property claimed on Line 390 of Form T661 must not be included on Schedule T2SCH8 (Capital Cost Allowance). While both new and used depreciable property meeting the ASA test can be included on Line 390 in the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool, under paragraph 2902(b) of the Income Tax Regulations used property (including demonstration equipment previously used regularly for any purpose prior to acquisition) is a prescribed expenditure that cannot earn an SR&ED ITC and must be deducted on Line 532 of Form T661—unless the used equipment underwent refurbishment by a vendor prior to acquisition so significant that it was brought to a "new state" (the current state of the art, evaluated by the proportion and importance of major parts replaced or rebuilt as new). If a claimant acquires used equipment and subsequently carries out significant refurbishments itself after December 15, 2024, only the costs of those subsequent refurbishments qualify for the ITC.

Under paragraph 37(8)(e) of the ITA, buildings or leasehold interests in buildings (other than prescribed special-purpose buildings) and amounts paid for the use of, or the right to use, a building are strictly excluded from SR&ED expenditures, while land and leasehold interests in land are excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures under subparagraph 37(1)(b)(ii). However, concrete footings, foundations, structural steel, stairs, and platforms used exclusively to support or provide access to SR&ED machinery are classified as CCA Class 8 machinery rather than part of the building and therefore qualify. Furthermore, prescribed special-purpose buildings approved under Section 2903 of the Income Tax Regulations qualify if first acquired after December 15, 2024, and constructed with working areas having a maximum structural displacement of 0.02 µm in any direction and an interior airspace containing, per 0.028 m³, fewer than: (a) 350 airborne particles ≤ 0.1 µm (and zero > 0.1 µm); (b) 75 airborne particles ≤ 0.2 µm (and zero > 0.2 µm); (c) 30 airborne particles ≤ 0.3 µm (and zero > 0.3 µm); or (d) 10 airborne particles ≤ 0.5 µm (and zero > 0.5 µm). Claimants must report detailed asset information for their 20 most expensive SR&ED capital expenditures in Part 6B of Form T661 (Box 780 property name, Box 782 full capital cost of acquisition including installation, customs/excise duties, and transportation, and Box 786 associated project numbers).
2. Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE) (Subsection 127(9) "qualified expenditure" (a)(iii) ITA)

Under the CRA's updated SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (revised May 22, 2026), new depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, that does not meet the ≥ 90% ASA test—and is neither General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF) nor Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP under Subsection 2900(11) ITR, such as equipment intended for commercial plant assembly/commissioning whose expected useful life is primarily commercial)—can qualify as Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE) on Line 504 of Form T661 if it is used primarily (more than 50% of its actual operating time) for SR&ED in Canada.

SUE eligibility is evaluated in two consecutive statutory windows based on actual operating hours rather than initial intent. First, First-Term SUE is evaluated over the "first period", which starts when the new equipment is acquired and available for use and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after that time. If actual SR&ED operating time exceeds 50% of total operating time during the first period, 25% (1/4) of the capital cost of the equipment qualifies for the SR&ED ITC. Second, Second-Term SUE is evaluated over the "second period", which starts when the equipment was acquired and available for use and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after that time. Provided the equipment qualified as First-Term SUE and its cumulative actual SR&ED operating time across the second period exceeds 50% of total operating time, an additional 25% (1/4) of the capital cost qualifies for the SR&ED ITC in that subsequent taxation year (for a combined maximum of 50% of the capital cost across both periods).

Unlike ASA capital equipment, the capital cost of SUE does not enter the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool; instead, the claimant depreciates the asset on Schedule T2SCH8 under standard CCA rules, and any SUE ITC claimed reduces the Undepreciated Capital Cost (UCC) of the CCA class in the following taxation year. Claimants must report the 20 most expensive SUE expenditures in Part 6C of Form T661 (Box 788 name, Box 790 purchase date in YYYY-MM-DD format, and Box 792 25% of full capital cost).
3. Equipment Lease Expenditures (SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy)

Under the CRA's updated SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (revised June 22, 2026), lease payments that first become payable after December 15, 2024, for equipment used in SR&ED in Canada are claimable on Lines 350, 355, or 360 (and listed per project in Box 759 of Part 6A of Form T661), with distinct rules depending on whether the claimant elects the Traditional or Proxy Method. Operating time for leased equipment is evaluated across the entire taxation year (and for taxation years straddling December 16, 2024, as a percentage of total operating time after December 15, 2024).

Under the Traditional Method (Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I) and (II) ITA), if leased equipment is used ≥ 90% (ASA) of its operating time in the taxation year for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost is claimed on Line 350. If leased equipment is used less than 90% of its operating time for SR&ED in Canada, the exact proportional percentage of SR&ED use can be claimed on Line 360 as an overhead and other expenditure, provided it satisfies the "directly related and incremental" tests under Paragraph 2900(2)(c) ITR. Under the Traditional Method, leased GPOEF and leased land also qualify if ASA or directly related and incremental.

Under the Proxy Method (Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) and (VI) ITA), if leased equipment (excluding GPOEF, buildings, and land) is used ≥ 90% (ASA) of its operating time in the taxation year for SR&ED in Canada, 100% of the lease cost is claimed (Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I)). If leased equipment (excluding GPOEF, buildings, and land) is used primarily—more than 50% but less than 90%—of its operating time in the taxation year for SR&ED in Canada, 50% (1/2) of the lease cost is claimed (Subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(VI)). If leased equipment is used 50% or less of its operating time for SR&ED, 0% can be claimed separately under the Proxy Method (it is deemed covered by the 55% PPA). Crucially, the CRA's SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy explicitly specifies that computers (including hardware, software, and ancillary equipment) and telecommunications bandwidth are not considered GPOEF and therefore qualify as eligible equipment leases under the Proxy Method.
6. Section 37 Deductible Expenditure Pool, ITC Recapture, and Unpaid Amounts
Continuity of the Section 37 Pool (Subsection 37(1) ITA)

Under the CRA's Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures Policy (updated March 27, 2026), subsection 37(1) establishes a cumulative, running-balance expenditure pool calculated in Part 3, Section C of Form T661. Under subsection 37(1.1), SR&ED performed by a corporate claimant is also considered related to its business if it relates to a business actively carried on by a related corporation (such as a wholly owned R&D subsidiary performing research for an operating parent corporation).

The Section 37 deductible expenditure pool is increased each taxation year by: (1) current SR&ED expenditures incurred in the year (Paragraph 37(1)(a), Line 380); (2) capital SR&ED expenditures incurred in the year for property acquired after December 15, 2024 (Paragraph 37(1)(b), Line 390); (3) repayments of government or non-government assistance that previously reduced the pool (Paragraph 37(1)(c), Line 445); (4) prior-year negative pool balances included in income under Paragraph 12(1)(v) (Paragraph 37(1)(c.1)); (5) prior-year SR&ED ITC recapture amounts and partnership ITC recapture excess amounts (Paragraphs 37(1)(c.2) and (c.3), Line 453); and (6) prior-year unused Section 37 pool balances carried forward (Line 450) or transferred upon an amalgamation (Paragraph 87(2)(l)) or wind-up (Subsection 88(1)) (Line 452).

Conversely, the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool is decreased each taxation year by: (1) government assistance and non-government assistance received, entitled to be received, or reasonably expected to be received (Paragraph 37(1)(d), Lines 429–432); (2) provincial super-allowance benefit amounts (Paragraph 37(1)(d.1)); (3) federal SR&ED ITCs applied against Part I tax or refunded in the immediately preceding taxation year (Paragraph 37(1)(e), Line 435—if the prior-year ITC exceeds the remaining Section 37 pool balance, the negative balance must be included in taxable income in the current year under paragraph 12(1)(v) and paragraph 12(1)(t) of the ITA, and is then added back to the pool in the following year under paragraph 37(1)(c.1)); (4) proceeds from the disposition of SR&ED capital assets (Line 440); (5) amounts deducted under subsection 37(1) in preceding years (Paragraph 37(1)(f)); and (6) insolvency deductions under section 61.3 (Paragraph 37(1)(f.1)).

A positive Section 37 pool balance never expires and can be carried forward indefinitely by a corporation or individual. However, a partnership cannot carry forward a Section 37 pool balance; under Paragraph 96(1)(e.1) ITA and the CRA's SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy, the entire pool must be deducted in computing the partnership's net income in the fiscal period incurred (and specified members of a partnership—passive partners not actively engaged in the partnership's business—are restricted in claiming partnership SR&ED allocations). If a corporation undergoes a loss restriction event (acquisition of control), a deemed year-end occurs and Paragraph 37(1)(h) and Subsection 37(6.1) reduce the pre-acquisition Section 37 pool to nil, unless the business in which the SR&ED expenditures were incurred continues to be carried on for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, in which case the pool can only be deducted against income from that same or a similar business. Similarly, an acquisition of control restricts the carryforward of pre-acquisition unused ITCs and the carryback of post-acquisition ITCs under section 127.
Investment Tax Credit Recapture (Subsections 127(27) to 127(36) ITA)

Under the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy and subsections 127(27) through 127(36) of the ITA, an SR&ED ITC is subject to recapture if, within 20 taxation years of earning the ITC, the claimant disposes of or converts to commercial use any SR&ED property—specifically materials transformed, ASA capital equipment, Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE), animals or growing things used in SR&ED, or physical property acquired under an SR&ED contract.

The recaptured amount is added directly to the taxpayer's Part I federal income tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion, and is equal to the lesser of: (1) the historical SR&ED ITC earned on the specific property (or the transferred qualified expenditure under a Form T1146 agreement pursuant to Subsection 127(28)), and (2) the historical ITC percentage (15% or 35%) multiplied by either the proceeds of disposition (if sold to an arm's-length purchaser) or the fair market value (FMV) of the property (or the product incorporating the transformed materials) at the time it is converted to commercial use or transferred to a non-arm's-length party (Subclause 127(27)(f)(ii)(B)). Recapture never applies to SR&ED salaries, overhead, or PPA, and does not apply to materials consumed (destroyed or rendered virtually valueless) unless scrap or insurance proceeds exceed 10% of the original material cost.
The 180-Day Unpaid Amounts Rule (Subsections 78(4) and 127(26) ITA)

Taxpayers must track two distinct 180-day payment rules at year-end. First, under subsection 78(4) of the ITA, any salary or wages incurred in a taxation year that remain unpaid on the day that is 180 days after the end of the taxation year are deemed not to have been incurred in that year for both the Section 37 pool and ITC purposes; instead, they are deemed incurred in the subsequent taxation year when actually paid (deducted on Line 315 in the year unpaid and added back on Line 310 in the year paid, though permanently excluded from the PPA salary base under Subsection 2900(9) ITR). Second, under subsection 127(26) of the ITA, current SR&ED expenditures other than salary or wages (such as materials, arm's-length contracts, overhead, or third-party payments) that remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year still enter the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool in the year incurred, but are excluded from qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes in that year (deducted on Line 520 of Form T661). When paid in a subsequent taxation year, they are added back to qualified expenditures in that later year (subject to the 80% limit if the unpaid amount was an arm's-length contract or third-party payment).
7. Government Assistance, Contract Payments, and Complementary Innovation Grants
Statutory Grinding Mechanics (Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsections 127(18)–(20) ITA)

To prevent double recovery on the same R&D expenditure, paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(18) of the ITA require a claimant to reduce both its Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and its qualified SR&ED expenditures by the amount of any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payment in respect of SR&ED that the claimant (or a non-arm's-length party under Subsection 127(19)) has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date for the taxation year. Where assistance is received by a non-arm's-length party, the parties may allocate the assistance among themselves using prescribed Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) under subsection 127(20). When a claimant subsequently repays government or non-government assistance (Paragraph 37(1)(c), Line 445 and Line 560 of Form T661), the repayment increases the Section 37 pool and earns an ITC at the historical rate of the year the assistance originally reduced the claim, though ITCs earned on repayments are non-refundable.

Under subsection 127(9), "government assistance" encompasses any grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, investment allowance, or other form of assistance from a federal, provincial, municipal, or foreign government, Crown corporation, or public authority, other than the federal SR&ED ITC itself and "excluded loans" defined in Subsection 12(11). Consequently, all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits (including Alberta's IEG and the R&D portion of Québec's CRIC) are government assistance that reduce federal qualified SR&ED expenditures in the year earned.

Where a claimant uses the Proxy Method, a portion of its provincial R&D tax credit is earned on the notional 55% PPA. Under the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, 100% of the provincial R&D tax credit (including the PPA portion) reduces federal qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(18). However, because the PPA is not an expenditure included in the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool, the portion of the provincial credit attributable to the PPA does not reduce the Section 37 pool under paragraph 37(1)(d); instead, that proxy-related portion must be included directly in taxable income under paragraph 12(1)(x) in the taxation year it is received. Furthermore, if a corporation is in a tax-loss position and cannot utilize a non-refundable provincial R&D tax credit (such as the 3.5% Ontario ORDTC, the non-refundable 10% BC credit, or the non-refundable 7.5% Manitoba credit), it may formally renounce that provincial credit on or before its filing-due date (6 months after year-end) so that the unutilized provincial credit does not grind its cash-refundable federal SR&ED ITC.
The CAE Inc. Precedent and the "Excluded Loan" Safe Harbour

A critical audit issue involves repayable government innovation loans. In CAE Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2022 FCA 178 (affirming 2021 TCC 57, 2021 DTC 1050; leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada denied May 26, 2023), CAE received $250 million in unconditionally repayable contributions from Industry Canada under the Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative (SADI), including $57 million in 2012 and $59 million in 2013, requiring CAE to repay 135% ($337.5 million) over 15 years at an implicit ~2.5% annual return. Both the Tax Court of Canada and the Federal Court of Appeal held that even though the arrangement was an unconditionally repayable loan rather than a forgivable loan, it constituted "government assistance" under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 12(1)(x) because the loan terms were concessional and driven by government policy covenants (such as maintaining manufacturing and IP in Canada) rather than ordinary commercial lending terms (applying Canada v. Consumers' Gas Co., [1987] 2 F.C. 60; Canada v. CCLC Technologies Inc., [1996] F.C.J. No. 1226; and Immunovaccine Technologies Inc. v. Canada, 2014 FCA 196).

To prevent bona fide government policy loans from wiping out SR&ED ITCs and triggering immediate income inclusions under paragraph 12(1)(x), Parliament enacted the "excluded loan" exception in subsection 12(11) of the ITA (effective for loans made after December 31, 2019), which excludes qualifying unconditionally repayable government loans from the definition of government assistance.
Stacking SR&ED with NRC IRAP and the Strategic Response Fund (SRF)

Canadian innovators routinely stack retroactive SR&ED tax credits with prospective direct government grants and contributions, subject to a general 75% cumulative government assistance stacking limit.

The most widely stacked program for small and medium-sized enterprises is the National Research Council of Canada — Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP). Administered through regional Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs), NRC IRAP reaches roughly 22,500 SMEs annually and funds approximately 3,360 incorporated, for-profit Canadian SMEs (with 500 or fewer full-time equivalent employees). IRAP provides non-repayable cost-shared contributions covering up to 80% of internal R&D technical salaries and subcontractor costs (typically for projects at Technology Readiness Levels TRL 3 to 7; median grant ~$75,000, with NRC published contribution decision authorities ranging from under $50,000 up to $10 million, alongside specialized streams including IRAP AI Assist, Defence Industry Assist launched in January 2026, and the NRC IRAP Clean Technology Renewal in Budget 2026). Unlike SR&ED (which is claimed retrospectively after year-end), IRAP must be approved before the project work commences. In computing the SR&ED claim on Form T661, the IRAP contribution is deducted as government assistance on Line 431 and Line 513, but under the Proxy Method, the claimant still calculates the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) on 100% of the unreduced gross SR&ED salary base before deducting the IRAP grant from total qualified expenditures.

For large-scale industrial R&D, the Strategic Response Fund (SRF)—rebranded from the Strategic Innovation Fund (SIF) and infused with an additional $1 billion over six years starting in 2028–2029 in Budget 2026 (within a $5 billion program envelope)—anchors transformative R&D, commercialization, AI, biomanufacturing, agri-food, and clean-tech industrial projects (minimum project size $10 million to $20 million+, with contributions starting at $10 million). Unless structured to meet the statutory "excluded loan" safe harbour under subsection 12(11) of the ITA, SRF contributions constitute government assistance that reduces qualified SR&ED expenditures.
8. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Ten Canadian jurisdictions—Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, Ontario, Québec, Saskatchewan, and Yukon—offer provincial or territorial R&D tax credits or grants that stack atop the federal SR&ED program. (Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do not offer a separate R&D tax credit). All provincial R&D tax credits reduce the federal Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and federal qualified SR&ED expenditures as government assistance.
1. Québec: The New Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC)

In its 2025–2026 Budget (Information Bulletin 2025-6, March 25, 2025), the Government of Québec enacted a sweeping structural consolidation of its innovation tax system for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025. Québec abolished eight legacy tax credits—including the R&D Salary Tax Credit (Form RD-1029.7), the University/Public Research Centre Tax Credit (Form RD-1029.8.6), the Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research Tax Credit (Form RD-1029.8.16.1), the Research Consortium Fees/Dues Tax Credit (Form RD-1029.8.9.03), the Technological Adaptation Services Tax Credit, and the Industrial Design Tax Credit—and replaced them with the single, unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC).

The CRIC is 100% refundable for all eligible corporations (and corporate members of eligible partnerships) operating a business with an establishment in Québec, eliminating the old corporate asset-size test. It provides a two-tier refundable credit rate based solely on spending volume: (1) a 30% refundable rate on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures exceeding the exclusion threshold (the $1,000,000 limit must be allocated among associated corporations carrying on business in Québec); and (2) a 20% refundable rate on all qualified expenditures above the $1,000,000 threshold, with no upper cap.

The CRIC covers two distinct activity streams carried out in Québec: (1) R&D activities, which are fully harmonized with the federal subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED (basic research, applied research, and experimental development), with the CRA continuing to perform the scientific eligibility review; and (2) eligible pre-commercialization activities undertaken in conjunction with and as a continuation of R&D work carried out in Québec by or on behalf of the corporation—specifically tests, technological validations, and studies performed to meet regulatory requirements and obtain an initial approval or certification for commercializing an innovation, quality control activities directly related to implementing a quality control system required for initial certification, and product design (including form and aesthetics, improved functionality, material selection, prototype development, usage scenarios, and pilot user validation).

Qualified expenditures for the CRIC include: 100% of salaries and wages paid to employees for eligible R&D or pre-commercialization work in Québec; 50% of amounts paid to subcontractors (arm's-length or non-arm's-length) for work performed in Québec; 50% of payments made to an eligible Québec public research centre, research consortium, or university entity; and 100% of capital property / equipment acquisition costs used in Québec for eligible R&D or pre-commercialization (excluding land, buildings, or rights to use land or buildings, and excluding property claimed under the C3i investment tax credit or a large investment project tax holiday; subject to a special recovery tax if the capital property ceases to be used solely in Québec within 730 consecutive days following the start of its use). Before earning the CRIC, a corporation's qualified expenditures for the taxation year must exceed an annual applicable exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the Québec Basic Personal Amount (BPA) of the personal income tax system for each employee ($18,571 for 2025; $18,952 for 2026), prorated by the time each employee spent on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities.

To claim the CRIC, corporations file Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (and Form RD-1029.8.PR for the pre-commercialization component, if applicable) alongside Form RD-222 (Deduction Respecting Scientific Research and Experimental Development Expenditures) and the Québec CO-17 return within 18 months of tax year-end. Crucially, only the R&D portion of the CRIC (reported on line 180 of Form RD-1029.8.CR and flowing to line 71 of Form RD-222 and lines 429a and 513 of federal Form T661) constitutes government assistance in respect of SR&ED that reduces the federal Section 37 pool and federal ITCs.
2. Ontario: Three-Pillar Corporate R&D Tax Credit System

Ontario's R&D incentives are codified in the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), S.O. 2007, c. 11, Sched. A, and are administered by the CRA through the T2 corporate return. Following the federal restoration of capital expenditures, Ontario updated its qualified expenditure rules so that 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024, qualify for Ontario R&D tax credits.

First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) (Section 96, Taxation Act, 2007; Schedule T2SCH566) provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit (reduced from 10% for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016) to qualifying corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (maximum annual cash refund of $240,000). Unlike the federal expenditure limit (which doubled to $6.0 million with a $15M–$75M phase-out), Ontario's OITC expenditure limit remains $3,000,000, and phases out linearly when prior-year federal taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 or when prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000 (shared among associated corporations and prorated for short taxation years).

Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) (Sections 38 to 45, Taxation Act, 2007; Schedule T2SCH508) provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (reduced from 4.5% after May 31, 2016) to all corporations with an Ontario permanent establishment on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (net of any OITC or OBRITC claimed on those expenditures), with no expenditure cap. Unused ORDTCs can be carried back 3 years and carried forward 20 years, are subject to recapture, and can be formally renounced by the filing-due date to avoid grinding the federal SR&ED claim.

Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) (Section 97, Taxation Act, 2007; Schedules T2SCH568 and T2SCH569) provides a 20% fully refundable tax credit on qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred in Ontario under eligible contracts with approved Eligible Research Institutes (ERIs), up to an annual expenditure cap of $20,000,000 per associated group (maximum annual refundable credit of $4,000,000).
3. British Columbia, Alberta, and Other Provincial/Territorial Regimes

In British Columbia, the BC SR&ED Tax Credit (Sections 97 to 103, Income Tax Act (British Columbia); Form T666), administered by the CRA, parallels federal SR&ED eligibility and expenditure limit rules. It provides a 10% tax credit (refundable for qualifying CCPCs up to their expenditure limit, and non-refundable for other corporations and above the expenditure limit; non-refundable credits can be carried back 3 years, carried forward 10 years, or renounced; subject to provincial recapture) and must be claimed on Form T666 within 18 months after the corporation's tax year-end.

In Alberta, the Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) (Sections 26.95 to 26.99, Alberta Corporate Tax Act; Information Circular IEG-1) is administered by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) for eligible R&D expenditures incurred in Alberta after December 31, 2020, matching federal SR&ED eligibility. The IEG provides a refundable grant on up to $4,000,000 in annual Alberta R&D spending, equal to an 8% base payment on eligible spending up to the corporation's base spending level, plus an enhanced 20% payment on eligible spending exceeding the corporation's base spending level. The filing deadline is 15 months after the corporation's filing-due date (21 months after tax year-end), and recapture applies.

In Manitoba, the Manitoba R&D Tax Credit (Section 7.3, Income Tax Act (Manitoba); Schedule T2SCH380), administered by the CRA, equals 15% of eligible Manitoba SR&ED expenditures made after April 11, 2017 (previously 20%). One-half of the credit on in-house R&D (7.5%) is refundable and 7.5% is non-refundable (while R&D under contract with eligible educational institutions is fully refundable); non-refundable credits carry back 3 years and carry forward 20 years, and can be renounced up to 1 year after the filing-due date for Manitoba purposes (or on or before 6 months after tax year-end for federal purposes). The filing deadline is 1 year after the filing-due date.

In Atlantic Canada, Nova Scotia (Section 41, Income Tax Act (Nova Scotia); Schedule T2SCH340) provides a 15% fully refundable corporate tax credit (filed within 18 months of tax year-end; subject to recapture; may be renounced within 6 months of tax year-end), and Newfoundland and Labrador (Section 42, Income Tax Act (Newfoundland and Labrador); Schedule T2SCH301) provides a 15% fully refundable tax credit to corporations, individuals, trusts, and partnerships (filed within 12 months after the filing-due date; provincial base is not reduced by government or non-government assistance except GST/HST input tax credits). In Yukon, the Yukon R&D Tax Credit (Schedule T2SCH442 for corporations; Form T1232 for individuals) is fully refundable at 15% of eligible Yukon SR&ED expenditures plus an additional 5% (20% total) on eligible expenditures paid or payable to Yukon University, filed within 18 months of year-end. New Brunswick (Schedule T2SCH360, subject to recapture) and Saskatchewan (Schedule T2SCH403, referencing a $1,000,000 threshold) also provide CRA-administered provincial R&D tax credits. New Brunswick provides a 15% fully refundable credit on eligible expenditures incurred after December 31, 2002, while Saskatchewan provides a 10% credit that, since April 1, 2017, is refundable for CCPCs on up to $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures per year, with the excess (and the expenditures of other corporations) earning a 10% non-refundable credit that can be carried back 3 years and forward 10 years.

body.text: 9. Governing Authorities, Prescribed Forms, Pre-Claim Approval, and Filing Deadlines
Statutory Filing Deadlines and the Zero-Discretion Bar (Subsection 37(11) and Paragraph 127(9)(m) ITA)

Under subsection 37(11) (for deducting or pooling SR&ED expenditures) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) (for earning an SR&ED ITC), a taxpayer must file prescribed Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND) for individuals and trusts) containing the "prescribed information" on or before the day that is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred. Because a corporation's T2 return filing-due date under Paragraph 150(1)(a) is 6 months after its taxation year-end, the statutory SR&ED reporting deadline for a corporation is 18 months after the end of the taxation year (except for tax-exempt non-profit SR&ED corporations under Paragraph 149(1)(j), which must file within 6 months of year-end under Subsection 149(7)). For an individual (sole proprietorship) carrying on a business, the T1 return is due June 15 of the following year, yielding an SR&ED reporting deadline of 17.5 months after the December 31 calendar year-end. For a trust, the T3 return is due 90 days after the trust's taxation year-end, yielding an SR&ED reporting deadline of 12 months plus 90 days after the trust's year-end.

As established by the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy (updated January 28, 2025) and consistently enforced by the Tax Court of Canada, the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline is a strict statutory bar: the CRA has no legal discretion to extend the deadline or accept late-filed prescribed forms. Filing a letter expressing an "intent to file" or submitting an incomplete form missing prescribed project descriptions or expenditure figures does not satisfy subsection 37(11). Furthermore, once the 18-month deadline has passed, a claimant cannot amend its claim to add new projects or increase/substitute expenditures to compensate for amounts disallowed during a CRA review. If Form T661 is filed on time but Schedule T2SCH31 is filed after the 18-month deadline, the expenditures still enter the Section 37 deductible pool, but no ITC is earned; conversely, if Schedule T2SCH31 is filed on time but Form T661 is filed late, the entire SR&ED claim and ITC are disallowed.
Architecture of Form T661 (Parts 1 to 10) and Claim Preparer Penalties (Subsections 162(5.1)–(5.3) ITA)

A complete Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim, accompanied by Guide T4088) comprises ten parts: Part 1 (General information); Part 2 (Project information in Sections A to C, subject to word limits; claimants with more than 20 projects may submit Part 2 upon filing for only their 20 largest projects in dollar value, provided they complete and retain Part 2 for all claimed projects at their place of business for immediate production upon CRA request and report all project costs in Part 6); Part 3 (Calculation of SR&ED expenditures in Sections A to C, including the irrevocable Traditional vs. Proxy Method election on Lines 160/162, allowable current and capital expenditures on Lines 300–400, and the Section 37 deductible pool continuity on Lines 429–460); Part 4 (Calculation of qualified SR&ED expenditures for ITC purposes on Lines 500–570); Part 5 (Calculation of the Prescribed Proxy Amount in Sections A and B); Part 6 (Project costs: Part 6A project cost breakdown including Box 759 lease costs; Part 6B top 20 ASA capital expenditures in Boxes 780, 782, and 786; Part 6C top 20 SUE expenditures in Boxes 788, 790, and 792); Part 7 (Additional statistical information); Part 8 (Claim checklist); Part 9 (Claim preparer information); and Part 10 (Certification by an authorized signing officer).

Under paragraph 37(11)(b) and subsections 162(5.1) to 162(5.3) of the ITA, Part 9 of Form T661 requires mandatory disclosure of every "claim preparer"—defined in subsection 162(5.3) as any person or partnership that accepts consideration to prepare or assist in preparing an SR&ED form (excluding an employee of the claimant preparing the form in the course of employment)—along with their billing arrangement. If Part 9 is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, subsection 162(5.1) imposes a $1,000 penalty, for which the claimant and the external claim preparer are jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable (subject to a reasonable due-diligence defence for the preparer under subsection 162(5.2)). Crucially, however, as clarified by subsection 37(11.1) and the CRA's updated SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy (January 28, 2025), Part 9 (like the deduction of a prior-year balance from the Section 37 pool) is not subject to the 18-month disallowance rule: an error or omission in Part 9 triggers the $1,000 penalty but does not disallow the underlying SR&ED claim.
The Streamlined 2026 SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval Process

Introduced in April 2026 and detailed in the federal government's 2026 Spring Economic Update, businesses can obtain binding upfront technical certainty before filing their tax return through the CRA's four-step SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval process:

items: Step 1 — Open a Pre-Claim Approval Request on Canada.ca: The business submits an initial online request form on Canada.ca. Existing SR&ED claimants in good standing with the CRA receive a case number in My Business Account within as little as 2 business days; new SR&ED claimants are contacted by the CRA by telephone within 5 business days.
Step 2 — Apply in My Business Account: The business completes the digital pre-claim application and uploads supporting technical documentation through My Business Account in just a few hours.

Step 3 — CRA SR&ED Specialist Meeting (Within 4 Weeks): Within 4 weeks of submitting the application in My Business Account, a 2- to 5-hour in-person or virtual meeting takes place with a CRA SR&ED specialist. This meeting is mandatory for new SR&ED claimants, but may not be necessary for existing SR&ED claimants in good standing.

Step 4 — Formal Pre-Claim Approval Determination (Within 8 Weeks): The business receives a formal written Pre-Claim Approval Determination from the CRA within 8 weeks of submitting its application in My Business Account.

body.text: 10. Audit Defence, Administrative Second Review, and Foundational Jurisprudence
CRA Review Procedures, Administrative Second Review (ASR), and Tax Court Appeals

When an SR&ED claim is selected for post-filing review, the CRA conducts a coordinated examination led by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) (who evaluates whether the work meets the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1)) and a Financial Reviewer (FR) (who audits the financial records, time sheets, payroll, contracts, and overhead allocations). Upon completing the technical review, the RTA issues a formal SR&ED Review Report (SRR) classifying each project under one of five determinations: AW (All Work), where all reviewed work meets the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1); SW (Some Work), where some reviewed work meets the definition of SR&ED and some does not; NW (No Work), where no claimed work meets the definition of SR&ED; UN (Unsubstantiated), where all claimed work cannot be substantiated; or AAF (Accepted As Filed), where work is accepted without a review to determine eligibility.

Under the CRA's Claim Review Manual, Financial Claim Review Manual, and Administrative Policy AP 2000-02R (Guidelines for resolving claimants' SR&ED concerns), the claimant is generally given 30 days (subject to reasonable extension) to submit additional documentary evidence or written responses to a draft SR&ED Review Report or financial review proposal. If disagreements cannot be resolved with the RTA, FR, and their immediate managers, the claimant may request an Administrative Second Review (ASR) before a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is issued.

Once the CRA issues a formal Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, the statutory dispute resolution timeline under the Income Tax Act governs. First, the taxpayer must file a Notice of Objection (Form T400A) with the CRA Appeals Branch within 90 days of the date of the Notice of Assessment or Reassessment. Second, if the CRA Appeals Branch confirms the reassessment, the claimant may file a Notice of Appeal with the Tax Court of Canada under either the Informal Procedure or the General Procedure.
Foundational Canadian SR&ED Jurisprudence
Canadian courts have developed a rigorous body of jurisprudence interpreting subsection 248(1), Section 37, and Section 127 of the Income Tax Act.

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), Judge Bowman (later Chief Justice of the Tax Court of Canada) established the foundational common-law test for SR&ED eligibility in Canada. At paragraph 16, Judge Bowman articulated the five-criteria test for SR&ED eligibility and outlined the five-stage scientific method process: (a) observation of the subject matter of the problem; (b) formulation of a clear objective; (c) identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty; (d) formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and (e) methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses. Crucially, Judge Bowman defined "routine engineering" as "techniques, procedures and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field," holding that technological uncertainty exists only where the problem cannot be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. He further held that the fact that the initial objective is not achieved invalidates neither the hypothesis formed nor the methods used—on the contrary, experimental failure often reinforces the measure of the technological uncertainty—and declared it "self-evident" that a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results must be kept as the work progresses.

In Sass Manufacturing Limited v. M.N.R., 88 DTC 1363 (TCC), the Tax Court of Canada established early in Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence that "systematic investigation" connotes the existence of controlled experiments and highly accurate measurements, involving the testing of theories against empirical evidence through repeatable experiments where the steps, changes made, and results are carefully noted—distinguishing eligible SR&ED from unrecorded shop-floor trial-and-error where the taxpayer provides no drawings, test reports, or evidence of a hypothesis. Subsequently, in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087, [1999] 1 C.T.C. 132 (FCA), the Federal Court of Appeal reversed a trial judge's overly rigid denial of an industrial R&D claim, distinguishing Sass Manufacturing on the facts while confirming that repeatability and verifiable evidence of testing are essential elements evaluated across the totality of the evidence.

In C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740 (affirming 2000 DTC 2372 (TCC)), the Federal Court of Appeal formally endorsed Judge Bowman's five Northwest Hydraulic criteria as binding appellate law across Canada. At the Tax Court level (2000 DTC 2372), the court also established a vital evidentiary rule highlighted in the CRA's Claim Review Manual: evidence of work done cannot rely on conjecture by an expert witness who was not directly or personally involved in the project to guess the problems encountered and steps taken simply by examining the end tools or results.

In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, 2021 FCA 88 (affirming 2019 TCC 246) and National R&D Inc. v. Canada, 2022 FCA 72 (affirming 2020 TCC 47), taxpayers whose claims were denied for lack of methodical experimentation and contemporaneous records argued before the Federal Court of Appeal that the third Northwest Hydraulic criterion (adherence to the scientific method) and fifth criterion (contemporaneous record-keeping) went beyond the text of subsection 248(1) or had been relaxed by the CRA's August 2021 eligibility guidelines. Writing for the Federal Court of Appeal in National R&D, Justice Rennie dismissed the appeal, holding that Kam-Press had settled that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria are the appropriate legal interpretation of subsection 248(1), that the CRA's 2021 guidelines did not remove the requirement to follow the scientific method, and that vague, unclear records failing to reflect a logical progression between the premise of an experiment and the result are fatal to a claim. National R&D also warned against submitting expert reports that purport to decide the ultimate legal question of whether work constitutes SR&ED.

In Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6 (and related Tax Court decisions on applied sciences), the Tax Court demonstrated the flexible application of the Northwest Hydraulic test to industrial and applied contexts, holding that a scientific or technological uncertainty can be established even where a publicly available solution or known preservative/component exists, provided it has never been used in the specific context and existing engineering knowledge cannot predict its behaviour. In the financial review domain, Oldcastle Building Products Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2016 TCC 183, and CalAmp Wireless Networks Inc. v. The Queen, 2013 TCC 201, govern the substantiation of SR&ED salary allocations, while Armada Equipment Corporation v. The Queen, 2007 DTC 879, and Val-Harmon Enterprises v. The Queen, 97 DTC 551, strictly enforce the "directly related and incremental" tests for SR&ED overhead expenditures under Paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the Income Tax Regulations. Finally, CAE Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2022 FCA 178 (affirming 2021 TCC 57; SCC leave denied May 26, 2023) stands as the controlling appellate precedent on government assistance under subsection 127(9) and paragraph 12(1)(x) of the ITA.
